dispute.riderClaim: My trip cost more than usual because the driver took a longer route than the app showed. Please refund the difference.
dispute.driverStatement: The rider asked me to go via Orchard Road. I told them it would be longer and cost more, and they agreed in the chat.

cases.summary: The rider claims the fare was higher than usual because the driver took a longer route than the app showed. GPS data confirms a material detour: the actual route was 9505 m versus a 7956 m reference, an excess of 1549 m (+19.5%), exceeding the RD-1 threshold of 796 m. However, the chat record shows the rider explicitly requested the Orchard Road route (CHAT-01) and, after the driver warned it would be longer and cost more (CHAT-02), the rider agreed (CHAT-03). Under RD-3, no refund is due when the rider requested or expressly approved the longer route. The rider's claim is therefore outweighed by their own approval, and the appropriate remedy is to keep the charge.

arguments.claim: The actual route was materially longer than the reference route, exceeding the RD-1 threshold by 1549 m (+19.5%).
The fare charged (S$12.98) reflects the longer distance of 9505 m, and the server-computed route-excess amount would be S$1.16 if a refund were due.

cases.summary: The rider expressly requested the Orchard Road route and approved the longer, more expensive fare in the in-app chat before the trip proceeded. GPS confirms a material detour under RD-1 (+1549 m, +19.5%), but RD-3 applies: no refund is due when the rider requested or expressly approved the longer route. The driver disclosed the longer distance and higher fare, and the rider agreed. The charge should stand.

arguments.claim: The rider initiated the route change by requesting to go via Orchard Road.
The driver expressly warned that the requested route would be longer and cost more, and asked for confirmation.
The rider expressly approved the longer, more expensive route before the trip continued.
The driver confirmed the agreed routing, so the deviation was rider-authorized rather than driver-initiated.
The fare charged matches the actual route and time and is arithmetically valid, so no billing error exists beyond the authorized detour.

The server-computed route-excess refund would be S$1.16 if RD-3 did not apply.

retrievedPolicies.ruleText: DEMONSTRATION POLICY. A detour is material when the actual route distance exceeds the reference route distance by more than the greater of 500 metres or 10% of the reference distance.
retrievedPolicies.remedyCriteria: Definition used by RD-2 and RD-5; no remedy on its own.

retrievedPolicies.ruleText: DEMONSTRATION POLICY. When a detour is material under RD-1 and neither RD-3 nor RD-4 applies, refund the eligible excess-distance charge: excess metres x per-kilometre rate x surge multiplier, capped at the surged distance charge and at the amount paid. The server computes the amount.
retrievedPolicies.remedyCriteria: refund_route_excess when RD-1 is met and neither RD-3 nor RD-4 applies.

retrievedPolicies.ruleText: DEMONSTRATION POLICY. No refund is due when the rider requested or expressly approved the longer route before or during the trip.

findings.claim: GPS-ROUTE shows the actual route (9505 m) exceeded the reference route (7956 m) by 1549 m (+19.5%), which is greater than the greater of 500 m or 10% of the reference distance, so the detour is material under RD-1.

The chat shows the rider requested the Orchard Road route (CHAT-01), the driver warned it would be longer and cost more (CHAT-02), and the rider expressly agreed (CHAT-03), with the driver confirming the agreed routing (CHAT-04); CHAT-SUMMARY records the rider route request and agreement with zero rider objections.

Because the rider requested and expressly approved the longer route, RD-3 applies and no refund is due, so the charge stands; the server-computed route-excess amount of S$1.16 is therefore not payable.

result.reasoning: The route deviation is material under RD-1: GPS-ROUTE shows +1549 m (+19.5%), exceeding the RD-1 threshold of 796 m. Ordinarily RD-2 would require a refund of the eligible excess-distance charge. However, RD-3 provides that no refund is due when the rider requested or expressly approved the longer route before or during the trip. The chat evidence is decisive: CHAT-01 shows the rider requesting the Orchard Road route, CHAT-02 shows the driver disclosing that it would be longer and cost more, CHAT-03 shows the rider expressly agreeing, and CHAT-04 shows the driver confirming the agreed routing. CHAT-SUMMARY corroborates a rider route request and rider agreement with no rider objections. RD-4 is not needed since RD-3 already resolves the case. Payment evidence (PAY-FARE, PAY-REMEDY) is available and the fare arithmetic is valid, so the case is not incomplete. Applying the policy literally, RD-3 controls and the remedy is keep_charge. History and risk signals are context only and were not used to establish fault.
result.riderExplanation: We reviewed your trip. The GPS data does show the route was longer than the app's reference route (about 1.5 km more, roughly 19.5%). However, the in-app chat shows that you asked the driver to go via Orchard Road, the driver told you it would be longer and cost more, and you replied agreeing to it. Under our route-deviation policy, when the rider requests or approves the longer route, no refund is due. The fare charged matches the route taken and is arithmetically correct, so the charge stands.
